claim: ERAT fluorescence shows nearly complete co-localization with ER-Tracker Red in H9 CHO cells.
source: Confocal analysis of ERAT fluorescence (Figure 1A, green) revealed nearly complete co-localization with the ER marker, ER-Tracker Red (Figure 1A, red)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: ERAT fluorescence shows nearly complete co-localization with the endogenous ER-resident protein PDIA6 detected by immunofluorescence.
source: Confocal analysis of ERAT fluorescence (Figure 1A, green) revealed nearly complete co-localization with the ER marker, ER-Tracker Red (Figure 1A, red), as well as with the endogenous ER-resident protein PDIA6 detected by immunofluorescence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and described in the text.

claim: Induction of F8 by SAHA treatment for 20 hr did not change the ER localization of the ERAT reporter.
source: Induction of F8 by SAHA treatment, an HDAC inhibitor, for 20 hr did not change the ER localization of the ERAT reporter (Figure 1B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The ER is not known to possess an independent ATP regeneration machinery.
source: As there is no known ATP regeneration machinery in the ER, and intracellular ATP regeneration from ADP takes place in mitochondria through OxPhos, and in the cytosol through glycolysis, it is of key importance to determine whether the ER ATP status depends on OxPhos and/or glycolysis (illustrated in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: 2-DG administration did not reduce mitochondrial respiration in H9 CHO cells when glucose and pyruvate were supplemented in the medium.
source: Importantly, with glucose and pyruvate supplemented in the medium to support mitochondrial respiration, 2-DG administration did not negatively affect the OCR, under both coupled and uncoupled respiration conditions (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A), suggesting that glycolysis inhibition by 2-DG does not acutely impair OxPhos in CHO cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by oxygen consumption rate measurements shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Oligomycin treatment immediately increased the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) in H9 CHO cells, reflecting glycolysis upregulation to compensate for ATP shortage due to OxPhos inhibition.
source: Interestingly, oligomycin (Oligo) treatment immediately increased the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) in H9 CHO cells, reflecting glycolysis upregulation to compensate for ATP shortage due to OxPhos inhibition, while 2-DG treatment inhibited this compensation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ECAR measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: All OxPhos inhibitors (oligomycin, rotenone, and FCCP) significantly decreased ER ATP levels immediately after administration.
source: All OxPhos inhibitors significantly decreased ER ATP levels immediately after administration, by analysis of ER ATP kinetics with time (Figure 1E) or by analysis at a single time point (15 min post treatment, Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1F.

claim: Bio-energetic inhibitors had no effect on ER localization of the ERAT probe.
source: Importantly, the bio-energetic inhibitors used had no effect on ER localization of the ERAT probe, as shown by confocal microscopy in H9 CHO cells co-transfected with a cytosolic RFP-based reporter, Cyto TagRFP (Merzlyak et al., 2007) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–F), and was further reflected by no change in the Pearson correlation coefficient under these conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data and Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Incubation with iodoacetamide (IAA) for 2 hr increased steady state ER ATP levels in H9 CHO cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: With this caveat in mind, it was particularly intriguing to observe that incubation with iodoacetamide (IAA), an inhibitor of glyceraldehyde phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH), for 2 hr increased steady state ER ATP levels in H9 CHO cells, in a dose-dependent manner (illustrated in Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Glucose supplementation had no effect on ER ATP levels in a defined medium with substrates supporting only OxPhos.
source: In an effort to further measure the extent by which glycolysis-derived ATP contributes to the ER ATP pool, we found that glucose supplementation had no effect on ER ATP levels, in a defined medium with substrates supporting only OxPhos (Figure 1H), while oligomycin strongly decreased ER ATP under these conditions (p<0.0001, with representative traces of raw FRET ratios shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 7A.

claim: 3-bromopyruvate (3-BrP) produced a similar ATP increase in the ER in a dose dependent manner.
source: In contrast, a third widely used glycolysis inhibitor, 3-bromopyruvate (3-BrP), produced a similar ATP increase in the ER, in a dose dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7B.

claim: Oligomycin or rotenone administration reduced steady state ER ATP levels in CHO cells that do not express human F8.
source: Finally, the observations made in H9 CHO cells were completely reproduced in CHO cells that do not express human F8 (Urlaub and Chasin, 1980), that is oligomycin or rotenone administration reduced steady state ER ATP levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 7D, indicated by red and orange curves).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7D and cited literature.

claim: Inhibitors of glycolysis, 2-DG or IAA, immediately increased ER ATP levels in CHO cells that do not express human F8.
source: In contrast, inhibitors of glycolysis, 2-DG or IAA, immediately increased ER ATP levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 7D, indicated by dark green and light green curves).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7D.

claim: Glucose supplementation significantly increased cellular ATP measured by luciferase assays.
source: As expected, glucose supplementation significantly increased cellular ATP measured (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A), and 2-DG decreased cellular ATP, while oligomycin only had a minor effect on cellular ATP compared to 2-DG (Figure 1—figure supplement 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8A.

claim: 2-DG decreased cellular ATP while oligomycin only had a minor effect on cellular ATP compared to 2-DG.
source: As expected, glucose supplementation significantly increased cellular ATP measured (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A), and 2-DG decreased cellular ATP, while oligomycin only had a minor effect on cellular ATP compared to 2-DG (Figure 1—figure supplement 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8B.

claim: 2-DG immediately decreased the cytosolic ATP/ADP ratio measured by flow-cytometry using the ratiometric PercevalHR probe.
source: Furthermore, 2-DG immediately decreased the cytosolic ATP/ADP ratio measured by flow-cytometry using the ratiometric PercevalHR probe (Figure 1—figure supplement 8C), while OxPhos inhibition by oligomycin did not significantly alter this ratio (Figure 1—figure supplement 8D), as previously shown by others (Imamura et al., 2009; Tantama et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8C and cited literature.

claim: OxPhos inhibition by oligomycin did not significantly alter the cytosolic ATP/ADP ratio.
source: Furthermore, 2-DG immediately decreased the cytosolic ATP/ADP ratio measured by flow-cytometry using the ratiometric PercevalHR probe (Figure 1—figure supplement 8C), while OxPhos inhibition by oligomycin did not significantly alter this ratio (Figure 1—figure supplement 8D), as previously shown by others (Imamura et al., 2009; Tantama et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8D and cited literature.

claim: OxPhos-derived ATP constitutes the major ATP supply source for the ER compartment.
source: To conclude, OxPhos-derived ATP constitutes the major ATP supply source for the ER compartment, while it is not possible to conclude whether ER ATP depends on glycolysis-generated ATP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the preceding sections.

claim: Application of the reversible SERCA inhibitor BHQ caused a rapid decrease in ER ATP in rat insulinoma INS1 cells.
source: Consistent with this notion, application of the reversible SERCA inhibitor, 2,5-di-(tert-butyl)−1,4-hydroquinone (BHQ), caused a rapid decrease in ER ATP in rat insulinoma INS1 cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The average of FRET over CFP ratios in the population of INS1 cells decreased and reached a plateau after 10 min post BHQ perfusion.
source: The average of FRET over CFP ratios in the population of INS1 cells decreased and reached a plateau after 10 min post BHQ perfusion (Figure 2C), and simultaneous measurement of ER Ca2+ by the D1ER probe (Palmer et al., 2004) in another set of INS1 cells confirmed the specific effect of BHQ on decreasing the ER Ca2+ concentration (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and cited literature.

claim: ER ATP levels did not completely recover after BHQ removal, while in the same time frame, the ER Ca2+ concentration returned to its basal level.
source: We observed that ER ATP levels did not completely recover after BHQ removal, while in the same time frame, the ER Ca2+ concentration returned to its basal level (compare Figure 2C–2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2D.

claim: The ER ATP levels took longer to recover when INS1 cells were monitored for up to 4 hr after BHQ withdrawal.
source: It is particularly interesting that the ER ATP levels took longer to recover when we monitored the INS1 cells for up to 4 hr after BHQ withdrawal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The recovered ER ATP levels in the same INS1 cells were reduced by a second BHQ stimulation, in an extent proportional to the levels of ER ATP recovery.
source: Furthermore, the recovered ER ATP levels in the same INS1 cells were reduced by a second BHQ stimulation, in an extent proportional to the levels of ER ATP recovery (compare Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: SERCA inhibition by Tg rapidly decreased ER ATP levels in H9 CHO cells.
source: In a similar manner, SERCA inhibition by Tg, an irreversible SERCA inhibitor, rapidly decreased ER ATP levels in H9 CHO cells, reflected by a decrease in the ratio of FRET-to-CFP fluorescence intensity measured by flow cytometery (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SERCA inhibition by Tg decreased ER ATP, independent of whether the extracellular medium contained Ca2+.
source: SERCA inhibition by Tg decreased ER ATP, independent of whether the extracellular medium contained Ca2+ (alpha MEM medium, 1.8 mM) (Figure 2E) or no extracellular Ca2+ (by 4 mM EGTA chelation, Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2F.

claim: Cyclopiazonic acid (CPA) induced a similar decrease in ER ATP at a dosage fifty times higher than Tg.
source: A third SERCA inhibitor, cyclopiazonic acid (CPA), induced a similar decrease in ER ATP at a dosage fifty times higher than Tg, presumably due to its low potency for inhibiting SERCA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The decrease in ER ATP by Tg correlated well with ER Ca2+ depletion as monitored by the GEM-CEPIA1er probe.
source: The decrease in ER ATP by Tg correlated well with ER Ca2+ depletion as monitored by the GEM-CEPIA1er probe (Suzuki et al., 2014) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and cited literature.

claim: The decrease in ER ATP upon Tg treatment preceded the decrease in mitochondrial ATP.
source: Comparison of the decrease in relative ATP levels triggered by Tg revealed that the decrease in ER ATP preceded the decrease in mitochondrial ATP (Figure 2G), refuting the notion that Tg decreases ER ATP by decreasing mitochondrial ATP.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing ER and mitochondrial ATP shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Tg treatment attenuated the decrease in cytosolic ATP/ADP ratio in H9 CHO cells.
source: In contrast, when the cytosolic ATP/ADP status was monitored by a structurally unrelated reporter, PercevalHR (Tantama et al., 2013), Tg treatment attenuated the decrease in cytosolic ATP/ADP ratio in H9 CHO cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2H and cited literature.

claim: Tg-mediated depletion of the ER Ca2+ store did not appear to increase ATP usage in the ER.
source: Tg-mediated depletion of the ER Ca2+ store did not appear to increase ATP usage in the ER since oligomycin treatment together with Tg reduced ER ATP only modestly, albeit significantly, compared to oligomycin alone (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Exogenously supplemented ATP in the perfusion buffer noticeably decreased the ER ATP pool.
source: Indeed, exogenously supplemented ATP in the perfusion buffer noticeably decreased the ER ATP pool (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The effect of exogenous ATP was neither reversed by addition of extracellular Ca2+ or washout of the agonist.
source: Furthermore, the effect of exogenous ATP was neither reversed by addition of extracellular Ca2+ (indicated by the blue bar in Figure 2J) or washout of the agonist, again demonstrating that Ca2+ mobilization lowers ER ATP levels in a sustained manner and supporting a 'memory' effect of the putative Ca2+ responsive ER ATP transporter.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: ATP import into the ER apparently requires a Ca2+ gradient (Ca2+ER > Ca2+cyto) across the ER membrane maintained by SERCA activity.
source: To summarize, ATP import into the ER apparently requires a Ca2+ gradient (Ca2+ER > Ca2+cyto) across the ER membrane maintained by SERCA activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the preceding sections.

claim: ATP trapped in the ER compartment accounts for the changes of luminescence signals above background in permeabilized CHO cells.
source: Using this system, we confirmed that only ATP trapped in the ER compartment accounts for the changes of luminescence signals above background (i.e., ER ATP), which was readily liberated by brief treatment with lipid-dissolving detergents (Figure 3A, p<0.001 and<0.0001 for Tween-20 and Triton X-100, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ATP generated by OxPhos from the permeabilized cells was evidenced by the higher ER ATP contents trapped inside PM-permeabilized cells, compared to the endogenous ATP found inside PM-intact cells.
source: In addition, ATP generated by OxPhos from the permeabilized cells was evidenced by the higher ER ATP contents trapped inside PM-permeabilized cells, compared to the endogenous ATP found inside PM-intact cells (Figure 3A, under 'Intact' group).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Addition of OxPhos inhibitors at the beginning of incubation reduced ATP luminescence to background levels in permeabilized CHO cells.
source: We also verified that ATP produced in this system was through OxPhos, as addition of OxPhos inhibitors at the beginning of incubation reduced ATP luminescence to background levels (Figures 3B and 1 µM 'Rotenone' or 'Oligomycin').
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Addition of Ca2+ (1 µM) significantly decreased ER ATP in permeabilized CHO cells.
source: Interestingly, addition of Ca2+ (1 µM) significantly decreased ER ATP (Figure 3B, p<0.0001 for '0 µM Ca2+' vs. '1 µM Ca2+' bars in the 'DMSO' group), suggesting that cytosolic Ca2+ inhibits ATP import from mitochondria into the ER.
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 1 mM EGTA significantly increased the ER ATP content in permeabilized CHO cells pretreated with Tg.
source: While 1 mM EGTA significantly increased the ER ATP content, addition of Tg had no effect (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: EGTA chelation increased ER ATP and adding CaCl2 back decreased the ER ATP in permeabilized CHO cells treated with ionomycin or Tg.
source: Again, the only effect we detected was with Ca2+ manipulation on the 'cytosolic' side of the ER membrane, that is EGTA chelation increased ER ATP and adding CaCl2 back decreased the ER ATP (Figure 3D, with free Ca2+ calculated to be 1 µM in presence of 1 mM EGTA).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knock-down of Slc35b1 in CHO H9 cells significantly decreased the baseline ER ATP level only in assay buffer containing no Ca2+, but not in presence with 1 µM Ca2+.
source: Consistent with the proposed role of an ER ATP/ADP translocase, knock-down of Slc35b1 in CHO H9 cells significantly decreased the baseline ER ATP level only in assay buffer containing no Ca2+, but not in presence with 1 µM Ca2+ (Figure 3E, p<0.0001 for '0 Ca2+' and non-significant for '1.0 µM Ca2+", respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The ER ATP decrease upon BHQ treatment was attenuated in HeLa cells upon Slc35b1 knock-down.
source: Similarly, using FRET-based microscopy in intact HeLa cells, we observed that the ER ATP decrease, after an initial increase, upon BHQ treatment was attenuated in HeLa cells upon Slc35b1 knock-down (by siRNA to 9.5%, compared to control siRNA treated cells) (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Slc35b1 knock-down abolished the ER ATP decrease as a result of OxPhos inhibition in HeLa cells.
source: Similarly, Slc35b1 knock-down also abolished the ER ATP decrease as a result of OxPhos inhibition (Figure 3G, by oligo plus rotenone).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A similar significant baseline ER ATP decrease after Slc35b1 knock-down was also observed for INS1 and H9 CHO cells using microscopy.
source: A similar significant baseline ER ATP decrease after Slc35b1 knock-down was also observed for INS1 and H9 CHO cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) using microscopy, while CaATiER was proportionally attenuated.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The CaATiER mechanism responded to Ca2+ concentrations ranging from 500 nM to 2 µM in semi-intact H9 CHO cells.
source: Interestingly, using semi-intact H9 CHO cells, the CaATiER mechanism responded to Ca2+ concentrations ranging from 500 nM to 2 µM (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B), with ATP content in the supernatant showing the opposite changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C, calibration provided in Figure 3—figure supplement 5D), further demonstrating that Ca2+ concentrations tested in our assay affected only ATP partitioning between ER and cytosol, but not mitochondria ATP production (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A, B, C, and D.

claim: The ER ATP decrease with increased Mg2+ concentration was negligible within a physiological range from 5 mM to 10 mM.
source: Finally, the ER ATP decrease with increased Mg2+concentration was negligible within a physiological range from '5 mM' to '10 mM' (p=0.21 by post-hoc t-test), confirming the decrease in ER ATP was specific to the Ca2+ cation.
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Ca2+ inhibits ER ATP uptake through a mechanism represented by SLC35B1.
source: In summary, based on the above results, we propose that Ca2+ inhibits ER ATP uptake (Figure 3H). In the CaATiER model, ATP from mitochondria is preferentially transported into the ER, possibly through a family of ER ATP transporter proteins represented by SLC35B1 (Klein et al., 2018), and the cytosolic Ca2+ concentration within this micro-domain attenuates ATP transport through a Ca2+ sensing component.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data and cited literature, illustrated in Figure 3H.

claim: SLC35B1 does not encode the Ca2+-responsiveness based on the lack of Ca2+-responsiveness from 10 to 50 µM when SLC35B1 was ectopically expressed in E Coli.
source: In addition, based on the CaATiER sensitivity to low µM of Ca2+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B), we predict that SLC35B1 does not encode the Ca2+-responsiveness considering the lack of Ca2+-responsiveness from 10 to 50 µM when SLC35B1 was ectopically expressed in E Coli (Klein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a prediction based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B and cited literature.

claim: ER stress was successfully induced by treating H9 CHO cells with HDAC inhibitors, such as SAHA or sodium butyrate (NaB), to increase F8 transcription.
source: ER stress was successfully induced by treating H9 CHO cells with HDAC inhibitors, such as SAHA or sodium butyrate (NaB), to increase F8 transcription from an HDAC-sensitive artificial promoter (Dorner et al., 1989) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A and cited literature.

claim: Pretreatment with 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (APB) successfully blocked Tg-triggered mitochondrial Ca2+ influx.
source: Pretreatment with 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (APB) successfully blocked Tg-triggered mitochondrial Ca2+ influx, although we cannot rule out the ability of APB to block other Ca2+ channels (Bootman et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and cited literature.

claim: ER stress induced by SAHA treatment did not alter mitochondrial matrix Ca2+ levels under resting conditions.
source: Although ER stress induced by SAHA treatment did not alter mitochondrial matrix Ca2+ levels under resting conditions, Tg-triggered mitochondrial Ca2+ influx was significantly more prominent in ER stressed H9 cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Tg-triggered mitochondrial Ca2+ influx was significantly more prominent in ER stressed H9 cells.
source: Although ER stress induced by SAHA treatment did not alter mitochondrial matrix Ca2+ levels under resting conditions, Tg-triggered mitochondrial Ca2+ influx was significantly more prominent in ER stressed H9 cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Neither the O-cresolphthalein (OCPC) chromogenic method nor the ER Ca2+ reporter (GEM-CEPIA1er) revealed a significant increase in the ER Ca2+ content in SAHA-induced H9 CHO cells.
source: The increased Ca2+ transfer into mitochondria was not due to an increased ER Ca2+ store since neither the O-cresolphthalein (OCPC) chromogenic method nor the ER Ca2+ reporter (GEM-CEPIA1er) revealed a significant increase in the ER Ca2+ content in SAHA-induced H9 CHO cells (Figure 4E and F), suggesting that the increased Ca2+ entry into the mitochondrial matrix under ER stress conditions is either due to enhanced Ca2+ mobilization from extracellular Ca2+ (Kaufman and Malhotra, 2014; Rizzuto et al., 2004) or the close proximity between the ER and mitochondria under prolonged ER stress (Bravo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by OCPC assay and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E and F, and cited literature.

claim: Oxygen consumption (by OCR) was not significantly different between ER stressed H9 CHO cells induced to express F8 and their un-induced counterparts.
source: At the same time, oxygen consumption (by OCR) was not significantly different between ER stressed H9 CHO cells induced to express F8 and their un-induced counterparts (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Seahorse flux assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: When F8 expression was induced by SAHA treatment, ER ATP homeostasis became more dependent on OxPhos.
source: Finally, when F8 expression was induced by SAHA treatment, ER ATP homeostasis became more dependent on OxPhos, as oligomycin treatment caused greater reduction in ER ATP for SAHA-treated H9 CHO cells compared to the un-induced H9 CHO cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Mitochondrial ATP levels were not affected upon induction of F8 expression.
source: This observation was not due to altered mitochondrial ATP supply (Figure 4G) as mitochondrial ATP levels were not affected upon induction of F8 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The ER ATP decrease in response to complete OxPhos inhibition was significantly more pronounced in SAHA-induced ER stressed H9 CHO cells than in vehicle-treated CHO cells.
source: Consistent with the ER ATP status measured by flow cytometry, the ER ATP decrease in response to complete OxPhos inhibition was significantly more pronounced in SAHA-induced ER stressed H9 CHO cells than in vehicle-treated CHO cells (quantified by maximal ER ATP reduction, Figure 4K, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4I, J, and K.

claim: The cytosolic ATP/ADP ratio decreased more quickly upon OxPhos inhibition in ER stressed H9 CHO cells induced by Tm.
source: Similar to the ER compartment, the cytosolic ATP/ADP ratio decreased more quickly upon OxPhos inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D), while no obvious difference was detected for the mitochondrial matrix ATP pool.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: ER stressed H9 CHO cells had significantly reduced glucose uptake independently of the F8 inducer, measured by 2-NBDG fluorescence assay.
source: Fully supporting the 'anti-Warburg effect', ER stressed H9 CHO cells had significantly reduced glucose uptake independently of the F8 inducer, measured by 2-NBDG fluorescence assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Only H9 CHO but not 10A1 CHO showed a significant reduction in glucose uptake in response to SAHA.
source: Notably, only H9 CHO but not 10A1 CHO showed a significant reduction in glucose uptake in response to SAHA, as the latter cells lack the HDAC inhibitor responsiveness and do not exhibit ER stress, as previously demonstrated (Dorner et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and cited literature.

claim: ER stress induced by a misfolded ER luminal protein causes metabolic changes, characterized by increased Ca2+ exchange between ER and mitochondria, increased dependence on ATP produced by OxPhos and by decreased cellular glucose uptake.
source: To summarize, ER stress induced by a misfolded ER luminal protein causes metabolic changes, characterized by increased Ca2+ exchange between ER and mitochondria (Bagur and Hajnóczky, 2017; Kaufman and Malhotra, 2014), increased dependence on ATP produced by OxPhos and by decreased cellular glucose uptake.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: ATP in the ER is mainly supplied from mitochondria.
source: By using a series of ATP and ATP/ADP ratio reporters to monitor real-time ATP changes in sub-cellular compartments and by complementary direct measurements of ER ATP, we observed that ATP in the ER is mainly supplied from mitochondria and that ATP homeostasis in the ER is maintained through a cytosolic Ca2+-antagonized ATP transport mechanism on the ER membrane (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: ATP homeostasis in the ER is maintained through a cytosolic Ca2+-antagonized ATP transport mechanism on the ER membrane.
source: By using a series of ATP and ATP/ADP ratio reporters to monitor real-time ATP changes in sub-cellular compartments and by complementary direct measurements of ER ATP, we observed that ATP in the ER is mainly supplied from mitochondria and that ATP homeostasis in the ER is maintained through a cytosolic Ca2+-antagonized ATP transport mechanism on the ER membrane (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The ATP level in the ER is insensitive to transient glucose deprivation and inhibition of glycolysis.
source: It was surprising that the ATP level in the ER is insensitive to transient glucose deprivation and inhibition of glycolysis, which causes an immediate reduction in cytosolic ATP.
evidence: This is a summary observation drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ATP exiting mitochondria immediately traffics through the ER ATP transporter(s), whereas ATP produced by glycolysis is spatially more distant to be efficiently captured by the ER.
source: Considering the close proximity between the ER and mitochondria (Scorrano et al., 2019), it is possible that ATP exiting mitochondria immediately traffics through the ER ATP transporter(s), whereas ATP produced by glycolysis is spatially more distant to be efficiently captured by the ER.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: An intimate cross-talk between ER protein misfolding and mitochondrial function could have evolved as a bioenergetic advantage for eukaryotes to develop into multi-cellular organisms.
source: Therefore, an intimate cross-talk between ER protein misfolding and mitochondrial function could have evolved as a bioenergetic advantage for eukaryotes to develop into multi-cellular organisms, in which cell-to-cell communications is necessitated by paracrine and endocrine signals.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: ATP usage in the ER is a key signaling event that controls mitochondrial bioenergetics, in addition to the signaling mediated by Ca2+ and reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Based on our findings, we propose that ATP usage in the ER is a key signaling event that controls mitochondrial bioenergetics, in addition to the signaling mediated by Ca2+ and reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Kaufman and Malhotra, 2014).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Cytosolic Ca2+ inhibits ATP import into the ER, indicating that a Ca2+ responsive element faces the cytosolic surface.
source: Our findings lead us to propose that cytosolic Ca2+ inhibits ATP import into the ER, indicating that a Ca2+ responsive element faces the cytosolic surface (Figure 3H), analogous to the mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter (MCU) gating system (Liu et al., 2016; Waldeck-Weiermair et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental findings and cited literature, illustrated in Figure 3H.

claim: Increased cytosolic Ca2+ reduces ER ATP usage to conserve ATP for cytosolic functions.
source: In summary, we propose that increased cytosolic Ca2+ reduces ER ATP usage to conserve ATP for cytosolic functions.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: Previous observations associating ER Ca2+ release with a transient ER ATP increase could reflect a temporary reduction in ER ATP consumption, rather than reflecting the luminal Ca2+ sensitivity of the ER ATP import machinery.
source: Previous observations associating ER Ca2+ release with a transient ER ATP increase (Vishnu et al., 2014) (and repeated in Figure 3F) could reflect a temporary reduction in ER ATP consumption, rather than reflecting the luminal Ca2+ sensitivity of the ER ATP import machinery.
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous findings in light of the current experimental data and cited literature.

claim: The ER preferentially depends on ATP produced from OxPhos.
source: Uniquely here, we demonstrate that the ER preferentially depends on ATP produced from OxPhos, which was further confirmed by our observation that ER protein misfolding in H9 CHO cells causes an 'anti-Warburg' effect.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ER protein misfolding in H9 CHO cells causes an 'anti-Warburg' effect.
source: Uniquely here, we demonstrate that the ER preferentially depends on ATP produced from OxPhos, which was further confirmed by our observation that ER protein misfolding in H9 CHO cells causes an 'anti-Warburg' effect.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Ca2+ exchange domain is not compatible with the ATP exchange domain between mitochondria and the ER.
source: While confirming the intimate functional cooperation of ER and mitochondria through exchange of adenosine nucleotides, our findings demonstrate that increased Ca2+ on the cytosolic surface of the ER membrane inhibits ER ATP import and predict that the Ca2+ exchange domain is not compatible with the ATP exchange domain between mitochondria and the ER, suggesting the existence of either A) Two categories of contact domains between the organelles, or B) A domain that operates in two distinct modes (Ca2+ exchange mode versus ATP exchange mode), which are temporally separated.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings.

claim: AMPK activation as a consequence of Ca2+ efflux from the ER can lead to compensatory mitochondrial ATP production in an attempt to resolve ER stress by supplying more ATP to the ER.

claim: The closer proximity between ER and mitochondria in ER-stressed CHO cells could ensure sufficient ATP uptake into the ER.
source: In our CHO cell model system, when Tg was applied to release ER Ca2+, the Ca2+ influx into the mitochondrial matrix was significantly elevated in ER-stressed CHO cells, which could reflect the closer proximity between ER and mitochondria to ensure sufficient ATP uptake into the ER (Kaufman and Malhotra, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: A highly efficient ATP supply mechanism exists between mitochondria and ER that is antagonized by cytosolic Ca2+.
source: To conclude, our results expand our knowledge of cellular bioenergetics by demonstrating that a highly efficient ATP supply mechanism exists between mitochondria and ER that is antagonized by cytosolic Ca2+.
